utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Could you we have the appearances, please, for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Carmela Javier and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thomas. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Boris Zorko, Chad Mair, Nadia Galinier, who is our new intern, Alex Fielding, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to point out that we have a lot of interference, a lot of buzzing in the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Interpreter. We'll try and -- is there anything we can do to help?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Technical department should know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith, do I call on you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Initially, we have a binder to present to the witness. Mr. Thomas has had an opportunity to look at the binder prior to the proceedings beginning today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you state your name for the record, please, and spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: My name is Jugoslav Kodzopeljic. J-u-g-o-s-l-a-v, Jugoslav. K-o-d-z-o-p-e-l-j-i-c, Kodzopeljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Sixty-nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was born in Kljajic, in the -- in Republika Serbia -- in Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you -- are you presently working or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was there a period of time when you were working for the military in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spent my entire professional career in the army, in the JNA and in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you retire, sir, from the army?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I retired in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to spend some time on briefly going through your military career. Could you tell us, apart from the educational part of your time in the army, what was your first duty in the army and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of a technical platoon in the communications regiment of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you use the term "technical platoon," could you explain to us what you mean by that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: A technical platoon is a unit in which an officer has to perform his duties as its commander and has two functions, that of supplying and that of maintaining equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you keep that position?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I occupied that position for a period of three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what period of time are we talking about with regard to this first duty? What years are we discussing here, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: From 1962 until 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thereafter, what was your next assignment, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was then appointed as the chief of the transport department in that very same unit, in that very same communications regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for what period of time did you occupy that particular position?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I occupied that position for about one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And thereafter, what was your next duty, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was then sent to the school of mechanics in Belgrade to pursue my studies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I take it you pursued your studies for some period of time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I graduated from the school of mechanical engineering in Belgrade in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After you graduated from the school of mechanical engineering in Belgrade in 1968, what post did you obtain in the army?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to the transport school in Titograd.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I was there until 1973.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in 1973, where did you go to next with -- in the context of your career in the army?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: In 1973, I was transferred to the technical department of the then-Federal Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how long did you maintain your position in the technical department of the - as you've put it - then-National Secretariat of Federal Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the time it was the Federal Secretariat for National Defence and later it was the Federal Ministry of Defence. I was there until the end of my professional career.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we go any further with regard to what your duties were in the technical department, when did the position change? And by that I mean, when did you change from being in the technical department of the National Secretariat for Defence to the, as you've put it here, secretariat for the -- I believe you said Ministry of Defence, but I could be incorrect. What year was that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to your working in -- in the technical department, what is the technical department? What are the duties and functions of the technical department?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The technical department has two main functions, generally speaking. It's responsible for all the equipment used by the land army, and in the tactical sense it's also responsible for a certain amount of equipment as is the case for all other tactical agents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you're referring to all of the equipment used by the land army, I take it that you are, by making that statement, excluding some aspects of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that is the tactical responsibility of the air force and of the navy was not something that we were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. And with regard to the issue of the statement you've made here which is "in the tactical sense it's also responsible for a certain amount of equipment," when you use the term "tactical," could you explain to us what you mean by that -- by that term in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, although it's a fairly broad area, but I'll try to give you an answer very briefly. As in the case of all other technical agents, for example, the use of -- in the case of the use of tanks, you have to deal with armoured vehicles. Well, in the case of my department, my department was responsible for systems that provided technical supplies for the land army, technical support for the land army. They provided electronic systems for the entire army and machinery for the entire army, apart for certain specific elements for the navy and for the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that you served in both the JNA and in the VJ. Could you tell us, when you began your service in the VJ or when you stopped your service in the JNA, what occurred, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the year. As far as the technical department is concerned, there were no changes with regard to its sphere of responsibility. All the tasks that we previously carried out were tasks that we continued to carry out in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you've said there. Without referring to a specific date at this time, can you tell us was there any particular event or series of events that caused you to change from being in the JNA to being in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the consequence of well-known events. Republics, certain republics, seceded, became independent. The SRJ became an independent entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "certain republics seceded," could you identify for us those republics that you're referring to when you say that certain republics seceded.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia, and the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is meant by "SRJ"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the FRY, F-R-Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what was the nation state that you were serving in the military called?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: It was called the SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before, as you've put it, secession of -- and I'm going to focus now on Slovenia and Croatia. Before the secession of Slovenia and Croatia, could you tell us what army was stationed in those republics?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: There were armies in the Republic of Slovenia -- or, rather, in all the republics. The 9th Army was in Slovenia. In Croatia there was the 5th Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the 9th Army and the 5th Army, were armies that belonged to what general army? What was the name of that specific army at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: It was an integral part of the army of the SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during that period of time, when the armies in Slovenia and Croatia were an integral part of the SFRJ, the military assets that existed in those republics belonged to whom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the common army of the SFRJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, those assets, and let's take for -- let's take Slovenia for an example, those assets that belonged to the army of the SFRJ, are those the kinds of assets that you're referring to when you discuss what your duties were in terms of technical administration?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the assets concerned, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And I take it that your answer would be the same with regard to Croatia in terms of the assets that were in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As you sit here today, do you recall whether or not the JNA - which is how I'm going to designate the army for the former republic of -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - left Slovenia at a particular time after Slovenia's secession from the country, the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that the JNA had withdrawn from Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when it withdrew from Slovenia, what, if anything, did it take with it, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The army took what it could take with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the balance of those materiels, do you know what occurred to those materiels and assets? Were they sold? Were they ceded over? Were they abandoned?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Those assets remained in the hands of the Slovenian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Croatia, what happened -- I should ask you the same question with regard to Croatia. When the JNA withdrew from Croatia, what did it do with its assets?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The situation is a little bit too complicated for me to explain, but I would like to say that the units or forces of Croatia also seized certain assets; first of all, those that -- well, the assets of the Territorial Defence, and then when they could enlarge the blockade, they took assets from JNA units. They also took what they could from JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I've been using the term in a very general sense here, that being the term "assets." Could you describe with some specificity, if possible, what the kinds of assets that we've been discussing involve?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Everything that is part of weapons and military equipment, all the sort of mobile assets for units and institutions within the army, the army of the JNA, of the SFRJ, all such assets that belong to that army. So we had infantry weapons, artillery weapons, armoured equipment. And then there were hospitals, rehabilitation centres, warehouses, depots. These were all the assets that the army had at its disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And at some point in time were you involved in preparing a report concerning assets that were left in the two respective republics that we've just discussed, Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I didn't directly participate in such an activity, but a colonel from my technical department was a member of the commission that worked on this and submitted such a report to the relevant authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the commission that you've just mentioned called, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I think it was a commission for the division of assets and liabilities, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recall, as you sit here today, who that report was submitted to? What was the purpose of that report?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The report was submitted to the international community. I can't remember who was responsible for that project on behalf of the international community at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. We have some -- some documents that go further into this particular report that we'll discuss momentarily. But at this point I'd like to move on. We'll come back to this particular issue. I know that we've in some senses jumped ahead it terms of -- in terms of your career, but let me ask you this: Between the time that you first became involved in the technical administration up until the time of your retirement, did you always maintain the same position within the technical administration, or did your positions change over time?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I started my work at the technical department from the lowest of positions, and I ended up as the head of the administration. Initially I was just a desk officer, then I was a senior officer, then I became the head of division, then I became the deputy head of the technical administration, and then in 1992 I became the head of the technical service, and in 1993 the head of the technical administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the technical service as opposed to the technical administration, could you explain to us what the distinctions are in terms of your duties between being the head of the technical service and the head of the technical administration?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can explain that. At one point, due to the downsizing of the personnel and the state itself, the air force technical, the navy technical, and the land technical services were pooled together, and at that period I was the head of the technical service and at the same time the deputy head of administration of the administration that was devised in that manner in that period, which meant that it compiled three services: air force, land, and navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the -- being the deputy head of the administration, what were your duties above and beyond, or were -- did you have any duties above and beyond those that you have discussed with us thus far?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: According to establishment, the chief of the first department is at the same time the deputy head of the technical administration. There are three departments in technical department in general. I was the head of the first department and the deputy head of the technical administration at the same time. So the deputy was not responsible for all the duties assigned to the technical administration except in the event when the head of the technical department is away or absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And at some point in time, if I understand your testimony correctly, you became the head of the entire technical administration?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That took place after these technical administrations were separated. I'm talking about the air force and the navy. I became the head of the technical department.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you became the head of the technical department, who were you subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: My superior officer was the assistant of the chief of General Staff for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: At the time, that was General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so we could focus in time, could you put a year on that, the year that you became the head?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was your relationship to the Ministry of Defence -- let me put the question to you in a different way. Were you or were you not subordinated to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: No. As the head of the technical administration, I was never subordinated to the Ministry of Defence, nor was the logistics sector subordinated to the ministry either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your -- to your knowledge, was there a difference or was the same structure in place before, and by that I mean under the SFRY, and after, under the FRY, with regard to the manner in which the Ministry of Defence and the army operated?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Changes were taking place. I can't remember when that occurred, but the General Staff became subordinated to the Ministry of Defence. However, in certain periods, the General Staff was practically independent, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: This is to the best of my recollection after 25 or 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And with regard to the -- with regard to the issue of financing for the army, were you involved in any aspect at all of planning for the financing or the budget of either - let me do this first - for the JNA. Were you involved in any of the planning for the budget for the JNA when you were working under the -- under the auspices of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that your volume be increased -- or, rather, the volume of the translation. I can't hear it very well. Yes. It's perfect now. Thank you. My administration, in all stages of preparing the budget, participated in compliance with the scope of our responsibilities; just like any other technical agent or strategical agent, the technical administration had to prepare an annual plan, to carry out analysis, and submit relevant reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in terms of the plan that you were involved in, what were the - and let me use this word to see -- or phrase to see if it works - what were the components parts that you considered in drawing up your plan?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, I can tell you that all army units and institutions of the SFRY and, at later period, FRY, who were integral part of the army and for which we were responsible in terms of providing technical support, all of this was within the scope of responsibilities of our planning duties. I'm not sure if I understood you correctly, if that is what you had referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You certainly did understand me in the most general of terms, because my question was put in the most general of terms. Let me introduce both a concept and a reality to you and see where we go from there. Dealing with the issue of logistics, could you first of all tell the Chamber what logistics entail, when that term is used.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: We didn't use the term "logistics." Our military system didn't function on the principles of logistics. We called that "rear support," and that meant providing technical support, transport support, medical support, civil engineering and construction support, and veterinary support. I believe I didn't omit any of the components.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that you didn't use the term "logistics" but you, rather, used the term "rear support." I'd like to go back in time with you just for a moment because you -- it seems that you're familiar with the term of "logistics." Was there a point of time in your career where you received any kind of training, specialised training, abroad?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I said that I went through all positions in the technical administration. At one point, I was the head of the department for development. And in that period I had a honour and a privilege to pay visits to certain armies in different countries, to become familiarised with their systems of technical support, i.e., logistics. I went to England, Germany, Russia, Greece, the Ukraine, and maybe some other countries where I learned about what they -- their concept of the job that we did was. And thanks to my predecessor, Admiral Praprotnik, who had been the head of the technical administration, we both studied the logistic systems, and at one point we even initiated the introduction of a logistic system rather than the rear support system. And it all went on until these events that we know took place and until my retirement. Our idea was to have such an organisation that would pursue the logistical logic, so to speak, of providing support to the army. Naturally, since I had the honour of having a Ph.D. and becoming a university professor, whatever I learned abroad I had an opportunity to teach in our schools and academies and in the course of conducting various courses all across the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, with regard to what you've just told us, did you learn about the NATO system of logistical support?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely the purpose of my visit with General Sljivic to England and Germany. Actually a whole group of us went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. This maybe self-evident, but was the SFRY part of NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: No. We have never been part of NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was the SFRY part of the Warsaw Pact?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was there a group of nations that you can identify that you were part of? And by this I'm asking whether you were a part of a group of non-aligned nations during the period of time that you were in the military with the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. My country was both a member and also part of the leadership of the non-aligned movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when the SFRY became the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I take it that your answer would remain the same; and by that I mean that you were -- your country was neither a member of NATO, nor was it a member of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Until I retired, we were neither a member of the NATO nor a member of the Warsaw Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just a brief digression. Are you aware of the Partnership for Peace programme which involves non-aligned nations becoming part of NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Look, the position of the head of the technical administration did not involve such matters. I can only tell you this as an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to you being an ordinary citizen later on in your testimony, perhaps. I want to return now, just for a moment, because I think we can at this time. If you would go to your binder, and you will see in your binder there are two sections: There's -- one section has an orange tab, a large tab divider, and then there's another section that has a green divider. And if you would go to the part of your binder that has the green divider in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could call up on the screen D609.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So if you would go to the -- I'm sorry. I do this all the time. It's 609D. If you would go to the -- flip your -- flip your binder to the green section. And perhaps the usher could be of some assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Thomas, you do confirm that you have seen that binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, we've previously discussed, in a brief sense, the issue of planning for the -- or assisting in the planning for the budget. And in that regard we've discussed the matter of logistics. With regard to the planning aspect of the budget, I'd like to focus your attention on the issue of something which were called "materiel lists," if I might. And what I'd like to do with you, if -- if we can, is get an understanding of what is the function of a materiel list and what is the procedure that is used with regard to materiel lists. I'm trying to figure out a way of doing this in an a relatively simple fashion. So, first of all, what I'd like to know is, if you could: Could you tell us what is a materiel list used for? Why do we have materiel lists in the army?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: May I make a few introductory remarks before I deal with that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that you can, if they're related to the issue of -- if it's the issue of materiel lists, yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are. In my country - and that's especially the case in the army - all equipment or state property, all socially owned property previously would be listed and recorded in relevant documents. So anything that a unit or an institution from the JNA or the Army of Yugoslavia had would have to be noted, recorded, in certain documents, and someone would be responsible for those records. Naturally, there are certain regulations according to which the officer in charge has the right to avail himself of certain equipment. He can categorise the equipment. And he can assign equipment and can sell such equipment. So all equipment in an army is recorded, and these records can be found in the relevant documents. So we have a list of everything, of all the equipment that the army has at its disposal, and this can be found in certain books, in digital form in computers, and at the relevant levels of command. The system in question is then checked and controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hold on for a minute before you go any further. You say the system in question is then checked and controlled. What are the -- what's the importance of checks and controls in the army with regard to the logistics that we're talking about? Why is that an important thing for an army to be able to do?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The state gives an army its property, makes it responsible for that property. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that it is used in an efficient and economic manner. Now, to attain this objective, to be sure that we know who has what at his or her disposal, to know whether something is being sent out of the system or is coming into the system, it is necessary to have materiel documents. There is a certain staff who are responsible for keeping records of such equipment. And as part of this record-keeping, as part of the system in question, we also have materiel lists that you have mentioned. So these materiel lists are part of the system. This means that nothing can leave a unit without this being reflected in the documents I have mentioned. Nothing can enter the unit; no logistical equipment can enter a given unit if it's not recorded in the relevant documents. So this then becomes part of the system, and then at any level of command it is possible to see who has what at his or her disposal. So the purpose of these materiel lists is to regulate the changes that take place within the system I have been describing to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue that we were discussing earlier, that being the issue of planning the budget, what importance, if any, do the materiel lists have with regard to those plans?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The materiel lists are important in that on the basis of these lists, the officer in charge drawing up a plan knows exactly what he has at his disposal, know what's coming according to the norms applicable to each unit and to each type of asset, and on the basis of that he can be able to draw up plans for the next year or for the next five-year period, as the financial plans were usually made for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in regard to what you've just said concerning drawing up a plan for the officer in charge, knowing exactly what is at his disposal, to what extent is the accuracy and completeness of those lists of any importance with regard to planning for the budget?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC

That means that according to their technical responsibility each individual knows what is within their purview and which assets they have been entrusted by the state to manage and run in a purposeful and economical way. I'm not quite sure if I gave you a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And when the -- when this particular form is filled out, could you tell us how many copies of the form are involved in one transaction? Is it a single piece of paper or multiple pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: This form is filled out in several copies. That has always been the case, regardless of the fact whether the bookkeeping is done on hard copies or on computers. However, as to the number of these MP-20 lists, depend on the type of transaction or, rather, the change to which the asset was subject: whether it was moving from one unit to another, from one army to another, whether it's been procured from abroad, whether it's been procured for a local factory, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when dealing with the issue of delivery, delivering, for example, let's say, one -- one gun, if you're moving a gun from one place to another, how many -- would there be -- well, that would be leading. I won't do that. How many sheets would be involved? Is it -- is it -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: At least five copies, sometimes even up to seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- let's use the five copies as an example. If there was a delivery of, for example -- let's make it -- let's say a hundred guns. Looking at that particular form, is that a form that would be used?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the form that an organ in charge would have to fill out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I seek the -- I seek its admission at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit D384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I ask that it be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be given -- marked for identification. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: If it assists, Your Honour, I have no difficulty with the document being admitted. It doesn't need to be MFI'd unless there's another reason to MFI it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we're okay then. It can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is I'd like to -- I don't know if we need to take a screen shot of this and do it again, because I'm going to use this same document a number of times. And if all goes easily and well, we will be doing this five times. If all goes easily and well. If not, we will revert to some other system. But this should work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the -- the number of forms, there were a minimum of five forms. And with Mr. Thomas's indulgence, I'm going to lead you just for a quick second in terms of -- if you could tell us the colour of the copies of the forms. Was -- and nothing more than that. The very first form on the top of the pile would be -- would it be white; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thereafter, there would be the same form that would be blue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He didn't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I thought he did. He nodded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I saw the nod.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You need to answer vocally, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the next form would be blue; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: At the time when I was working at the technical administration, we had one white, one blue copy, and the rest of the copies were pink.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it at the time that you were working at the technical administration the paper itself had the ability to be written on in the first copy, and whatever was written on the first copy would go through the balance of the copies. Like carbon paper. Old school.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the time and the speed of movement of these forms. However, initially, each copy had to contain the initiation of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The first copy, the white copy, in terms of the white copy, what information would be filled out on the white copy with regards to the delivery of the - as we put it - 100 guns. And if you could look at the form, and with the assistance of Madam Usher and the magic pen that we have, if you could put a tick mark in each of the boxes that would be filled out by the person who is entering data into the white copy.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Could we please increase this by 25 per cent? [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if we can increase it by -- yes, it seems to be getting -- good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On my screen it has remained the same. It's not enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, can you -- if you can work with it -- if you can work this screen for this particular form, that'll be great. We'll see what we can do about increasing it for you on the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the witness not have this document in hard copy in his binder? Can't we use the ELMO if he wants it bigger?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's actually an excellent idea. And we have -- and if it's not in his binder, we have another copy of it in hard copy. Considering the effort that the gentleman's going through. I suggest that we follow the Chamber's suggestion and move to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Usher is busy doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Madam Usher, here. We have another copy of it. You could show it to -- if you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I marked this in colour red, but I don't know if it's visible everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if the Chamber -- if the Chamber's able to see it, then we can continue in this way. Or we can -- we can just move to the ELMO and hard copy, if that makes it easier for all people to see it. And I think it might, noticing the way they were all leaning over the screens. Madam Usher, if I might give to you, initially, two markers. One is yellow, one is orange. Yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could go through -- if you could go through the same exercise once again, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the -- is there anything at the bottom? There may be something on the bottom of the screen. But just staying at the top of the screen for the moment, you've marked a number of boxes, and are those the boxes that are filled out by the sender of the materiel? And in this instance it would be the hundred rifles that we've discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I'll have to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: This materiel list can be filled out -- or, rather, let's begin like this: Let's say that the materiel is either in a depot or in a unit. Now, if the officer in charge of that depot issues an order, it is him who is going to fill out as I have marked on this form. Now, that is sent to his depot. And, of course, there are people in the depot who are handling these army assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a quick question, which is with regard to box number 24, 25, and 26 on the form, which is, What is box number 24 for? What information is filled out in box number 24?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: It's a very important piece of information for the system of materiel bookkeeping. The nomenclature number of the JNA is entered there and the name of the asset. So it's not enough to say "gun this and this." You need to enter a 12-digit number. This 12-digit number gives you an exact identification of which particular asset is in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you refer to the ELMO, which is the other -- which is the hard copy, and in box number 24 put in the words "12-digit number." In box number 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- put in "12-digit number."

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect, yes. And that's the thing you're talking about when you're referring to a nomenclature that has to be identified, the specific item that is being delivered or transferred?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In box number 25, is there a particular designation that goes into that particular box?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Since we are talking about computerised bookkeeping, codes are entered here, referring to certain measures. For example, you use pieces. Kilogramme would be designated by another number, et cetera. This is also very accurately specified in the nomenclature so that you know always exactly which unit of measure is applied. You cannot express everything in kilogrammes, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you're dealing with, for example, pieces, unit pieces, what number would be -- what would you be using?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And box number 26 is for what purpose, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: All pieces of equipment and materiel, with a view of keeping records with regard to replenishment and their quality. And there's a specific instruction to identify the category and quality; for example, there's a category which says "New asset." And then after a few years it will move to category 2, et cetera. So in this box you enter the data that the service has with respect to the category of a particular asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And can you give us an example of a category of a particular asset that you would enter in that box? You have 60 here, so what would you enter in the next box, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: For example, if you say guns, if they're fully combat ready after they had been repaired, they would be marked as category 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, with regard to the boxes that you have placed yellow markings, are those the entirety of the boxes that are marked by you in which data is entered in the first instance in the white copy, or are there other box that also are dealt with in the white copy?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: This has been done by an organ who initiates this list and issues an order. Now this is dispatched to the depot people who have to implement that physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when it's dispatched to the depot people who have to implement the order physically, what, if any, boxes do they put any information in to indicate that they have, in fact, implemented, physically, the order? Or put in other terms, they've done what they're supposed to do by virtue of the order they've been just given.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: They have to fill out the following boxes: Number, date, signature, professional service organ, and the commission that is supposed to put this into practice. This has to be signed by the order issuer, the handler, and the -- those amending the form number 50 by way of reducing the quantity that had existed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you do us a favour and please -- please mark in yellow those boxes that you've just put a dot in.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned -- you mentioned, I believe, the word "commission," which is in box number 35. What is the commission that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I have to explain this. Sometimes one person can deal with equipment being handed in, and sometimes it's the commission. Usually for complex equipment you have the commission that is involved. So it's the commission of a warehouse or of a supply unit that does this work, and they physically deliver the item to the relevant person, or they send it for transport by rail or by some other means or to some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the white form, the first form that we've been discussing, are there any other entries on that form in order to indicate that it is a completed transaction up to this point, that all the parties have done what they're supposed to do? And by that I'm referring to any kind of stamps or any other entries that are put on the form.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: According to the instructions for materiel auditing, all parties involved in this procedure have to certify their signature with a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And where would that certification occur?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Under 37. The person issuing the order has to certify the procedure with a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you do us the kindness of taking the pen and drawing a circle to indicate the stamp, where the stamp would be.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks] -- I apologise. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see that you've -- you've -- you've indicated, I take it, that the place where you've drawn the black circle is incorrect and the stamp should be up above where you've presently drawn a circle in yellow; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Where it's written "MP," the stamp rubric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarity, if you would draw a red -- a red circle over where the yellow circle that you just drew was, so we know that that's -- just --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. There we go. And that would be the stamp; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who retains this copy?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: It depends on the situation, and the situations can be of various kinds. But, in general, this form, this pink form and four copies, a blue copy and four pink copies, forwarded -- are sent into the system. So this official only has one pink copy at his disposal, only retains that pink copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And who retains the white copy? We haven't got to the pink copies yet, but who retains the white copy?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The white and blue copies and a certain number of pink copies are forwarded into the system. One pink copy accompanies the goods, the equipment. It's either transported by train, or it's taken by the person who came to take charge of the item in question. Or the person who takes charge of the asset retains one pink copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to the asset -- the asset being sent out, does the -- does the manager of the warehouse from where -- from the place where the goods were sent retain a copy, one of the pink copies that you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. One pink copy remain in the warehouse, in the supply unit. And on that basis, in column 39, this is noted. The 100 guns in question are noted as having been deducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I can hand you another blank copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Put that on top. It will it be -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- this will be the pink copy that you just referred to. I take it that all of information that you have mentioned that is filled out on the white copy is also filled out on the pink copy. And in addition, there are certain boxes on this pink copy that are filled out by the -- what I'll call the warehouse manager; is that correct? Now, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This only concerns column 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you take the orange pen and just put a marking on -- on box 39.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. This then has to do with a different form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you do me the kindness of -- at the top of the form, write the word "pink," since you've indicated this is a pink copy.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the materiel --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we to understand that these copies are really not copies of one another? There is certain information that goes on certain colour copies and certain information that goes on other colour copies? And I ask this because of the question you asked by saying, at line -- page 41, line 9: "... in addition, there are certain boxes on this pink copy that are filled out by ... what I'll call the warehouse manager; that is correct?" Providing the context of what you said earlier, I'm left with the impression that this information that you're referring to on that sentence was -- is not contained in the white copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be correct, Your Honour, with regard to the box that he's filled out on the first pink copy. That would be box 38. That would not be kept on the white copy. So the white -- the white copy -- if we were to have him fill in all of the parts of this pink copy, he would have -- there would be yellows in all of the areas where he's put them on the white copy, which I'm more than happy to have him do so you can see the difference of the way that it would look, because -- visually, since we're dealing with five copies. But that would be new information. The white copy would only be in yellow. The first pink copy that we discussed has the new addition of the information that is in orange, which is someone's signature. And this is for a tracking device so you can see with regard to the -- now the issue of who would handle the materiel in the warehouse. The way that that's understood is by that particular box being filled out. Now, I hope that's clear. Because if it's not clear, I want to make sure it is clear because ultimately we're going to be dealing, specifically, with the materiel lists that the Prosecution has introduced in this case and have a discussion about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I want to make sure that -- I want to make sure that the system is understood first so that when we actually get to the materiel lists that have been introduced by the Prosecution, the Chamber has an appreciation of what the system is that should have been utilised, what is the methodology that's used, what are the requirements therein, in a physical fashion, so that you can see what the positive and negative aspects are to the forms that the Prosecution has introduced. Because we obviously contend there's certain matters that need to be discussed, but I'm not going to go -- that -- we'll take that no further at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For purposes of clarification, because it might be of some assistance, with regard to the pink copy that you have of right now, which is the pink copy that is, as I understand it, retained by the manager of the warehouse, could you -- could you fill in the boxes in yellow that you had previously filled in in the white copy to show the progression of the delivery.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: There's a little difference. All five copies have been filled in in an identical manner so far, but the fifth copy, which remains in the warehouse, in that case, column 39 doesn't have to be filled in because when the equipment and records are sent out, no one has to know where he made a record of everything. So all four copies are sent on, but one accompanies the goods being delivered. And three copies, the white copy, the pink one, and the blue one, are sent to the command of the unit that is to receive the equipment in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. With that explanation, let us now move to the blue copy. With regard to this particular copy, this is a copy -- who -- who has physical possession of this copy? Is this the person who receives the goods?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure you've understood me. All three copies, the white one, the blue one, and one pink copy, are sent to the unit, to the command of the unit who is to receive the items in question. So all three copies are sent there. And at that point, well, they're sent to the command. He doesn't have to receive this on the very same day. He doesn't have to receive the guns on the same day. He waits for the post, for this to arrive. When it arrives, he asks his manager whether -- or his officer whether he has received this. He brings the list and says, "Yes, I've received it." And then he fills in this right-hand corner at the top, and that concerns all three copies that are used by the person or the official receiving the assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you there. With regard to -- this will be the blue copy. With regard to the blue copy, if you could first of all put at the top of the page "Blue."

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you had indicated that the receiver fills out a certain number of the boxes. Could you use that particular marker and draw a line in the boxes that are filled out by the receiver.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could stop you there. Are there further box that are filled out -- I saw that you were about to fill out another box -- further boxes filled out by the receiver?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: It depends on the type of transaction, on whether payment has been made or not. There are certain other columns for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the very bottom of the form, which boxes in the bottom of the form are filled out by the receiver?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular form, which is the blue form, is the information that is contained on the left-hand side of that form information that has been filled out as well? And that was information you had previously filled out in yellow. Could you please take the yellow --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you please take the yellow marker and, using the yellow marker, fill in those boxes.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: This is filled in by the sender.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe that you'd indicated, with regard to the sender, there was a stamp on -- there was a stamp on the signature. Could you use the red pen, once again, and show us where the stamp would be.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the sender. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Wait a minute. Hold on. Hold on --

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Or the receiver.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So you've now -- you now have -- you've marked two circles in red, both which indicate stamps, one for the sender and one for the receiver; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so we're clear about this particular copy which we've called the blue copy, the information that was filled out by the sender is in yellow, the information that was filled out by the receiver is in green; right?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: That's how the form has been, in fact, divided, if you have noticed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you go to the very bottom of the form. With regard to boxes number -- box number 38 -- or I may -- I don't know if it's 38 or 39. I'm not sure. Now, that's the form -- don't use the red pen. With regard --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Take that pen away from that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to those particular -- those particular boxes, are those boxes also filled out on the blue form as you had previously done, I believe, in orange? They were signed. 38 and 39. 38 and 39.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: 38 and 39. This has to be filled in by the sender, the official in charge of the assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, are there any further forms that are filled out with regard to this particular transaction? Because you'd mentioned there were a number of pinks. Is there another pink form, then, that has further information from the information that we find on the blue form?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure you've understood me correctly. The white copy, the blue one, and the pink one are sent to the command of the unit receiving the assets, and one pink copy remains in the hands of the manager, of the official who received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's understood. Now, we haven't filled that form out yet, have we? The pink form that remains in the hands of the manager that receives it.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you put on the top of this form "Pink 2," using the -- now -- don't use orange. Let's use -- don't use orange. Here, use the blue pen. Now, with regard to this form, all of the information that we have discussed that was filled out on the blue form would also exist in that form, which we'll do at the very end. And, in addition, is there any further information that is filled out on pink 2?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The only difference is that it is audited. We're talking about box 42, because he has his books, his archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we could move that further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you said 42, could you put an X in that box, 42.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to boxes 40 and 41, when are those boxes filled out?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: These boxes are filled out in all four -- three forms. It depends on who -- on whether the person who brought the goods brought that form too. So either three or four forms are filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With all of these forms filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think, with the Court's indulgence as well as Mr. Thomas, he can fill the form out -- the balance of the form in the break, and we'll check it, rather than taking up the time to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With this form now being filled out, is the transaction completed for the purposes of accounting? Are all the forms that are necessary done so that the delivery can be tracked?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, these three forms, the white one, the blue one, and one pink form, are sent to the person who received it for materiel auditing. The white and pink copy are certified. They're filled in. The pink one is filled in, too. And then, in an identical manner, he certifies that the goods, the assets, were received. Having received the relevant information, these forms are sent on. The pink form is sent to the person who sent the goods, the assets; the white copy is retained by the official; and the pink copy is retained by the technical department or the person who is in charge of logistics supplies in the unit. On the basis of these two documents, the white one and the pink one, an entry is made in the books. An entry can't be made in the books until the receiver says that these items have been listed in the book. Once this has been done, then the process, the transactional process, is completed, the one that concerns the warehouse and what was delivered by the warehouse, because -- perhaps I haven't said this: The white copy is sent by the receiver to his accounting department. The pink one is given to the sender who sends the copy to his own auditing department.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: Once this transaction is completed, how many different points are there, for purposes of double-checking, to make sure that the asset claimed to be sent was in fact received or the asset alleged to be received was in fact sent? How many different places can you look at to make sure that that's occurred? And what I'm looking for here is a question -- a system of checks and balances here that you were talking about in terms of the importance of accuracy in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: There would be a minimum of five such points and perhaps even six.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue that we were talking about at the beginning, which is planning for the budget, is this information information which is critical for purposes of that planning, to have these forms accurately filled out and be in a position to know and to be able to track whatever the particular piece of -- of equipment is?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Why do I say four, five, or six, or a minimum five and perhaps even six? Well, because some of the documents remain in the units that are -- handed over the equipment or received equipment. Some documents go to the centre in the relevant -- at the relevant level of control and command. One report goes to the Ministry of Defence where the situation, with regard to the equipment, can also be checked in regard to the units concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Hopefully we've made things clearer, but perhaps we have not. What I'd like to do is ask you the following question with regard to the number of forms that the accounting department needs in order to verify that a transaction has occurred, and by that I mean that a piece of equipment has gone from the sender and been received properly.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Provided I managed to explain the procedure to you, although I'm not an expert in dealing with these documents, but I have been using them in my system, I would like to say that the blue copy is kept by the materiel bookkeeping of the sending unit; the white copy is retained by the receiving unit; one pink copy is held by the handler who had handed over the asset; and the other pink copy is kept by the handler who received the goods. And they are used for entering changes in their records, that is to say, on MP-10 form. As I said in the course of transfer, one of the documents may accompany the asset, and this copy is maintained by the technical service organ in the receiving unit, purely for keeping records. So it is not particularly important, but is, nevertheless, necessary as an element of the transaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just looked at your last answer, and I'm a bit confused. I -- you indicated the blue copy is kept by the sender and the white copy is retained by the receiving unit. I had thought that it was the reverse of that. That this was, in fact, the white copy that was retained by the sender and the blue copy that was -- the blue copy that was the receiving unit's copy. Am I incorrect in that?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: What I have just said is correct. The blue one is kept by the sender, and the white one is kept by the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the issue of the budget and planning the budget, these materiel lists have what significance? Are they necessary in order to plan the budget?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: The materiel lists as documents, from the moment that something is being sent by the sender and received by the recipient, they are no longer significant in the sense of information exchange because the respective centres, the bookkeeping centres, have exact data about who sent what and who received what. Therefore, one can keep these forms for a certain number of years and thereafter are destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what the significance is, if any, where the form is not filled out completely and accurately with regard to the data that is necessary for planning the budget? And I'm referring to the kinds of things that you're doing in terms of understanding what assets you have available, what assets have been used, what assets have been transferred, what assets have been retained.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you this: That the accuracy of keeping records of this nature and their processes in financial centres is something that the system of materiel transactions is very much dependent upon in the army. And as far as I know, the same applies to state assets. One must treat military assets in this way, otherwise it is impossible to implement any command unless this procedure is adhered to in a very precise and accurate manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to go back to something that we were referring to before because I understand that it's now available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we please have 1301D on the screen. I believe that was where we left off, and I'm using -- this was the last document that was introduced in evidence -- introduced into evidence MFI'd; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd just like you to take a look at this document for a quick second, just to focus you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could we now take a look at 1303 D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Previously when we were referring to this report, do you recognise this document as being one of the documents that you were discussing in terms of the issue with regard to assets in the Republics of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is an integral part of the report sent to the international community for the purpose of the division of assets and liabilities, and this is a summarised review for a particular addressee that is indicated on the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move its admission on the same terms and conditions that were previously discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is now 13012, or what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is 1303.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us be very precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were. We're referring to numbers. It's perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Are we talking here about the review of movable and immovable assets?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. The document 1303D is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be Exhibit D385, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith, you are aware and you do remember that 1301D has not been tendered. You said -- you asked the witness just to have a brief look at it and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd been informed that it had been tendered. If it'd not been tendered, I move its admission under the same terms and conditions as previously sought. And I do apologise to the Court if I've missed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It is indeed D383, marked for identification. Sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Too many documents this morning, Your Honour. Fortunately they're not all -- fortunately they're not all forms. I'm now going to ask you to call up 1308D. And, Mr. Registrar, for your purposes, I'll be calling up 0910, 11, and 12 in order, to make your life a bit easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that your response would be the same with regard to this -- this document, which is part of that same report.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's part of the same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move its admission under the same terms and conditions. And ask Mr. Registrar to pull up the next document after the Court has ruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D386, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And you said the next document is 0910?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 1309. It was -- it's going to be -- Your Honour, it's going to be 1309, 1310, 1311, and 1312 sequentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, I assume that your answer will be the same, which is this is -- this is part of that same package that we were referring to before.

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have just only received it on my screen. Yes, yes. It's the same report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. But may I just be clear what it is. We've just had a summary of assets left in Croatia moved and now we've got this one, which is not a form, which is actually 1309D. Is it this one or the previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It should be a form, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's the previous one, which is the one about Croatia. That's right. This one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. That's 1309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Okay. This one is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit D387, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for purposes of focus and clarification, the next document which would be 1310 refers to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a summary of military facilities from that same report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might ask a question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- is this equipment left in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the ABiH Army or with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you hear His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. I thought His Honour gave the floor to you. This is a summary of immovable assets of the JNA, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as at 31st December, 1990. That was the situation that prevailed at the moment prior to any events taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that answer, but His Honour has asked you a different question which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think my question becomes irrelevant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, actually, you anticipated my question at the conclusion of all of these documents. If we could -- if we could now have 1311D on -- I need to move this to admission under the same terms and conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given the same conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P388 [sic], marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say "P," Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. It would be D388, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 1311D, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This refers to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JUGOSLAV KODZOPELJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's from the same package of the estimation of the value of assets as at 31st of December, 1990, that is to say, the value of the military assets that the army had at its disposal and that the army managed in that particular republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move its admission under the same terms and conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D389, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have 1312D.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
